name: Brow lamination kit
lead: A brow lamination kit is a set of chemical solutions that relaxes the keratin bonds in eyebrow hairs so they can be brushed upward and outward and held in a uniform, fluffy direction. The process is comparable to a hair perm. Results are commonly said to last about four to six weeks. Lamination is sold as a salon service and as at-home kits.

A 2025 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology states it is the first to address possible side effects of brow lamination, and it calls for more studies and regulation. No controlled trials of lamination outcomes were identified, and eye-care commentary describes comparable risks from related lash perms and tints. [1][2]

paras: A kit generally contains a lifting (reducing) lotion, a setting (neutralizing) lotion, a nourishing oil or serum and applicators. The brow hairs are brushed into the desired direction, treated with each solution in sequence and cleaned. Brow lamination is often combined with tinting in salons.

Hair keratin is held in shape by disulfide bonds. A reducing agent, commonly a thioglycolate such as ammonium thioglycolate, breaks the bonds so the hair can be repositioned, and a neutralizer re-forms them in the new arrangement. [1]
Eyebrow hair is short and has a brief growth phase, and reference sources describe a growth cycle of about three to four months, which relates to how long a new shape persists as hairs shed. [3]
The effect on appearance, a fuller, more uniform and upswept brow, is described by practitioners and users. It has not been quantified in published trials.

The 2025 review reports that ammonium thioglycolate and thioglycolic acid are hydrophilic and can be absorbed through skin by intracellular and transappendageal routes, and that they can cause allergic contact dermatitis with irritation, dryness and erythema. The authors also discuss effects on hair shape, structure and pigmentation and describe possible systemic effects involving reproductive, ocular, respiratory and endocrine systems, while stating that further studies are needed. [1]

An optometry clinical report on cosmetic eye enhancements describes chemical irritation and injury risks from products used near the eyes, and a case report describes allergic dermatitis and periorbital swelling after permanent eyelash dye. Experts quoted in such commentary advise patch testing and describe at-home use as higher risk than professional use. [2][4]

Lamination is discussed as a way to give brows a groomed, upswept look without makeup. Consumer discussion in beauty forums includes questions about doing it at home. [5] The site rates it as having a strong but temporary effect.
No studies found that test brow lamination for appearance outcomes. A 2025 review summarises toxicological and dermatological data on the thioglycolate ingredients used in the technique. [1]

timeline.event: First review of potential side effects of brow lamination published. [1]
